title: Assignment 2
text:
In Teaching to See, Andrei Severny and Edward Tufte, building on the insights of Inge Druckrey, emphasize the art of truly learning how to observe visual form. One of the first lessons from Druckrey is the distinction between thin and thick, as well as curve and linearity. These contrasts are more than stylistic choices; they establish rhythm, balance, and structure in design. A thin line may suggest delicacy or subtlety, while a thick stroke conveys weight and emphasis. Similarly, curved forms add movement, grace, and fluidity, while linear elements ground a composition with stability and direction. Training the eye to perceive these subtle relationships develops sensitivity that is essential for effective visual communication.
Holmes extended this idea by reflecting on the relationship between the eye and the hand in writing. He described the eye as the organ of selection and judgment, the part that perceives form, proportion, and harmony. The hand, in contrast, serves as the instrument of execution, translating visual thought into physical marks. Writing and drawing, therefore, require an intimate collaboration: the eye directs and evaluates, while the hand follows and shapes. This duality highlights that skill in design is not just manual dexterity, but also cultivated vision.
The influence of such training can be seen in modern technology. Steve Jobs often credited a college calligraphy course for shaping his design sensibility and inspiring the Macintosh computer’s typographic elegance. Calligraphy taught him the beauty of proportion, spacing, and detail, which later translated into Apple’s groundbreaking use of digital fonts and aesthetically refined interfaces. For Jobs, calligraphy represented the fusion of art and technology—a philosophy that made Apple products not only functional but also visually compelling and deeply human-centered.
A final lesson from Druckrey and Tufte concerns the difference between geometric accuracy and optical accuracy. Geometric accuracy refers to strict mathematical precision—perfect circles, exact squares, or measurable alignments. Yet, design that is only geometrically correct can often feel awkward to the human eye. Optical accuracy, by contrast, adapts form to perception. In typography, for example, curved letters like “O” often extend slightly beyond a baseline so that they appear equal in size to straight letters, even though they are not geometrically identical. This principle reflects a core truth: design is judged not by mathematical rules alone but by how forms are perceived in real experience.
In sum, Teaching to See underscores that design begins with perception, sharpened through attention to contrast, balance, and the collaboration of eye and hand. From Druckrey’s lessons on thin and thick to Jobs’ appreciation for calligraphy, the text reminds us that clarity, elegance, and human perception matter more than mechanical precision. Seeing, in this sense, is not a passive act but an active discipline that shapes the way we create and communicate in the visual world.

title: EPPS6356 — Assignment 1 (Data Visualization)
text:
#Reading Assignment- Francis J. Anscombe (1973). Graphs in Statistical Analysis. The American Statistician, 27(1), 17–21.
Anscombe (1973) showed that four extremely different datasets can share nearly identical summary statistics (means, variances, correlation, and the same least‑squares regression line). However, when we graph, the results are totally different.From this, the most important point is that we should never rely on numbers alone: we must always visualize. Practical solutions include (i) always starting with basic exploratory plots (scatterplots, residuals, boxplots), (ii) checking model assumptions with diagnostics, (iii) considering robust methods or transformations to address outliers and nonlinearity, and (iv) documenting how visual findings inform model choice and interpretation. To conclude, visualization is not optional—it is essential to statistical thinking.
#Illustration; The chunk below recreates the quartet and shows the same regression line over four extremely different patterns.


Code
# Base R ships with 'anscombe'
df_list <- lapply(1:4, function(i) {
  data.frame(
    x = anscombe[[paste0("x", i)]],
    y = anscombe[[paste0("y", i)]],
    set = paste("Set", i)
  )
})
ans_df <- do.call(rbind, df_list)

# Fit a single (illustrative) regression per set
coefs <- by(ans_df, ans_df$set, function(d) coef(lm(y ~ x, data = d)))
coefs <- do.call(rbind, coefs)

text:
Summary and Review for The Future of Data Analysis (Tufte, Edward,2016)
The talk opens with David Smith’s personal story about discovering Edward Tufte’s The Visual Display of Quantitative Information, framing data science as the union of computation and the craft of communicating evidence. Tufte then lays out four threads (1) exemplars of excellence in visualization; (2) the ethical imperative to “get it right” in analysis; (3) a sharp separation between confirmatory (pre-specified, unhacked) and exploratory (detective) work; and (4) his current research on “the thinking eye,” the interface between light, perception, and reasoning.
Drawing on Galileo’s “visible certainty,” Tufte argues that strong visuals convert speculation into evidence. He highlights a public-health project that digitized decades of MMWR data to show the dramatic, time-aligned impact of vaccination—an example where scale + design yield persuasive causal narratives. He contrasts this with failures: the Phillips Curve’s collapse outside a cherry-picked window; fMRI software that produced high false-positive rates; and Google Flu’s overfit, opaque model. The lesson: overfitting, researcher degrees of freedom, and p-hacking make many published findings untrustworthy.
As remedies, he points to institutional designs that reduce analytic freedom at the point of confirmation: FDA requirements to pre-specify tables, models, and outcomes; political science journals accepting registered reports before analysts ever see the data. Exploration is still valuable—but its patterns should be independently replicated on fresh data. He also emphasizes data forensics as a communal, open-source discipline (not “secret sauce”) to catch mundane but consequential errors (e.g., Excel row limits, type coercions, missingness).
On visualization craft, Tufte’s north star is content-driven design with high information throughput: maps as everyday exemplars; Swiss topographic cartography as “gentle 3D” that integrates words, numbers, and depiction without clutter; multi-view explanation (video, slow-mo, stop-action) for events like a soccer goal; and screen real estate (4K/5K/8K) as an underused affordance for seeing “big data” in one analytic frame. Practical heuristics: show causality (annotated linking lines; verbs, not nouns), show comparisons (“compared with what?”), and privilege substance over style (zero chart junk).
The final arc, “the thinking eye,” centers on disciplined skepticism: constantly ask “How do I know that?”; beware survivorship bias; remember that metrics are gamed; go into the field to observe how data are truly generated; and structure your day to protect deep work (“real artists ship”).
Review. The talk’s strengths are its synthesis of epistemology, institutional design, and graphic craft—and its specificity. Instead of generic “be ethical,” we get operational fixes (pre-registration, independent replication, shared forensics checklists). The visual exemplars are well-chosen: they demonstrate density without clutter and connect design choices to cognitive tasks. If there’s a limitation, it’s that some cases (e.g., MRI and Google Flu) are presented briskly; a few technical footnotes on what precisely failed (e.g., multiple-comparison correction assumptions, feature leakage) would help practitioners prevent repeats. Still, the overarching argument—separate exploration from confirmation; make the pipeline auditable; design for reasoning—is clear and compelling.
Reflection. Three takeaways I’d apply immediately:

Pre-commit where it matters. For confirmatory studies, write analysis plans, model formulas, and primary tables before touching the data; park all post-hoc ideas into an “exploratory” appendix and seek replication on fresh samples.
Design to answer a verb. Every figure should complete a sentence like “X causes Y” or “X increased after policy Z”—with annotations, aligned timelines, and explicit counterfactual or comparison groups. If the figure can’t support the verb, redesign it or change the claim.
Raise the information ceiling, not the ink. Prefer one rich, labeled, multi-layered view over a carousel of minimalist charts. Use large canvases, quantified typography, and integrated labels; avoid decorative 3D but embrace “gentle 3D” when it encodes real structure.

Personally, the reminder to go see how measurements are made is catalytic: many “mystery” artifacts in code are traceable to messy collection practices. And the daily habit advice—start with the work, not the feed—aligns with doing careful, reproducible analysis. In short, the talk re-centers data science on its first principles: evidence over assertion, explanation over performance, and designs that help the eye think.

Summary of Podcast “Next Industrial Revolution is Industrial AI” by Barbara Humpton & Olympia Brikis
Artificial intelligence is a powerful transformation in manufacturing and industry and often known as industrial AI. Siemens USA leaders Barbara Humpton and Olympe Brinkus emphasize that AI is enabling tasks once impossible. The example of those impossible tasks includes predicting machine failures, shifting from mass production to mass customization, and creating digital twins of products, plants, and entire systems. What’s more, we could see an automotive manufacturer where AI-powered visual inspection replaced manual checks and the result is that every door met a defined standard of “perfect”. We now see that Siemens’ Amberg plant in Germany transitioned to full automation where staffs are handling cognitively demanding tasks aided by generative AI assistants. Industrial AI applications range from predictive analytics that prevent equipment breakdowns to generative design that proposes innovative solutions.To implement projects with AI, first step to do is capturing usable data, then adding sensors to older machines, and setting clear goals such as improving throughput, quality, or energy efficiency. But one thing to consider is job loss case for human resources. Instead of investing in human, Siemens invested $37 million annually in training and fostering multi-generational teams. All in all, Barbara Humpton highlights the potential for AI to spark innovations in materials, medicine, and global problem-solving. Olympe Brinkus noted that democratized access to AI tools will open doors for a more diverse workforce on the rise of specialized AI models trained on proprietary industrial data than internet-scale datasets, promising more precise, domain-specific solutions.

EPPS 6302 - In-Class Hackathon  Brief 
Our code successfully queries the collection of 100 congressional hearing records related to the U.S. assistance to Ukraine, although the files for this hearing are large that the final download of all 100 files are 479 documents with only five fails, which were anything hearing that was related to the U.S. Courts. Our code used three libraries: httr (to make the API calls), jsonlite (to handle JSON data from the API), and dplyr (for data manipulation). Our team successfully set our parameters with each with our own GovInfo API key to collect congressional hearings from the “Foreign Relations Committee Ukraine assistance” search query to allow for max documents set of 100, and to load and saved directly to our local directory in folder ‘US_UkraineAssistance’. Our code three core functions are the search_govinfo(), which submits a query to the GovInfoAPI to retrieve the documents, secondly it uses download_documents(), which goes through the list to fetch the corresponding files to save them into our folder, and finally creates_summary() which joins the search, download statuses for the final report and CSV summary file. Since, the API call required to download large documents, the total time is estimated twelve hours to retrieve all queried documents. 
AI USE: Our Team used Claude AI Sonnet 4.5. The prompt we used: “Provide a beginner starter code inserted the In-class Hackathon: Government data file.” The second prompt was interpret each error we receive such as the “Error in search_govinfo(SEARCH_QUERY, API_KEY, MAX_DOCUMENTS) : API request failed with status: 400.” The third was  prompt was to share with Claude the code so it could find any mistakes or miscode to solve the object query errors.  
Review and Revise: Our team made sure that Claude provided us starter and simple code, it limited the review and revise to simple code name changes and the correct link to data.gov to provide the search query to Ukraine foreign assistance and for assistances on error interpretations. 
R code are as follows
rm(list = ls()) # ============================================================================= # GovInfo API Document Collector # Purpose: Search and download Foreign Relations Committee documents # =============================================================================

Load required packages
library(httr)
library(jsonlite) library(dplyr)


=============================================================================


SETUP: Configure your API key and search parameters


=============================================================================
API_KEY <- “wrTOFJGtYuZENTHmQfQNxonXssS4OOqPbonAg7gm”
COLLECTION <- “CHRG” # Congressional Hearings collection SEARCH_QUERY <- “Foreign Relations Committee Ukraine assistance” MAX_DOCUMENTS <- 100 DOWNLOAD_FOLDER <- “US_UkraineAssistance”


=============================================================================


STEP 1: Search for documents and get list


=============================================================================
search_govinfo <- function(query, api_key, max_results = 100) {
cat(“Searching for documents…”)
# CORRECT API endpoint - requires POST with JSON body base_url <- paste0(“https://api.govinfo.gov/search?api_key=“, api_key)
# Build JSON request body request_body <- list( query = query, pageSize = min(max_results, 100), offsetMark = “*” )
cat(“Searching for:”, query, “”)
# Make POST request with JSON body response <- POST( base_url, body = request_body, encode = “json”, content_type_json() )
# Check if request was successful if (status_code(response) != 200) { cat(“Error! Status code:”, status_code(response), “”) cat(“Response content:”, content(response, “text”), “”) stop(“API request failed with status:”, status_code(response)) }
# Get the response content response_text <- content(response, “text”, encoding = “UTF-8”)
# Check if it’s actually JSON (not HTML) if (grepl(“<!DOCTYPE”, response_text) || grepl(“<html”, response_text)) { cat(“ERROR: Received HTML instead of JSON”) cat(“First 500 chars:”, substr(response_text, 1, 500), “”) stop(“API returned HTML instead of JSON - check your endpoint URL”) }
# Parse JSON response data <- fromJSON(response_text)
# Extract document information if (!is.null(data\(results) && length(data\)results) > 0) { documents <- data$results
# Make sure we have the required columns
if (!"packageId" %in% names(documents)) {
  cat("Available columns:", paste(names(documents), collapse=", "), "\n")
  stop("packageId column not found in results")
}

# Select available columns
cols_to_keep <- c("title", "packageId", "lastModified", "governmentAuthor1")
available_cols <- intersect(cols_to_keep, names(documents))

documents <- documents %>%
  select(all_of(available_cols)) %>%
  mutate(doc_number = row_number())

cat("Found", nrow(documents), "documents\n")
return(documents)
} else { cat(“No documents found”) return(NULL) } }


=============================================================================


STEP 2: Download documents


=============================================================================
download_documents <- function(doc_list, api_key, folder) {
# Create download folder if it doesn’t exist if (!dir.exists(folder)) { dir.create(folder, recursive = TRUE) cat(“Created folder:”, folder, “”) }
cat(“documents…”)
# Track successful downloads download_status <- vector(“list”, nrow(doc_list))
# Loop through each document for (i in 1:nrow(doc_list)) {
package_id <- doc_list$packageId[i]
cat(sprintf("[%d/%d] Downloading: %s\n", i, nrow(doc_list), package_id))

download_url <- sprintf(
  "https://api.govinfo.gov/packages/%s/pdf?api_key=%s",
  package_id,
  api_key
)

filename <- paste0(folder, "/", package_id, ".pdf")

# Try to download
tryCatch({
  response <- GET(download_url, write_disk(filename, overwrite = TRUE))
  
  if (status_code(response) == 200) {
    download_status[[i]] <- list(
      packageId = package_id,
      status = "success",
      filename = filename
    )
    cat("  ✓ Success\n")
  } else {
    download_status[[i]] <- list(
      packageId = package_id,
      status = "failed",
      error = status_code(response)
    )
    cat("  ✗ Failed (status:", status_code(response), ")\n")
  }
  
  # Be nice to the API - add small delay
  Sys.sleep(0.5)
  
}, error = function(e) {
  download_status[[i]] <- list(
    packageId = package_id,
    status = "error",
    error = as.character(e)
  )
  cat("  ✗ Error:", e$message, "\n")
})
}
